open_questions: High-resolution imaging or on-target time series at the measured centroid offset can confirm whether the dip is on the neighbour at 18-21" that requires only a 7-23% eclipse.
dossier.public_summary: The dip does not line up with the target star; difference imaging puts it about 10 arcseconds away and the depth swings wildly between sectors. Two nearby stars within one TESS pixel can make the shallow 1.5 Earth-radius signal with a small eclipsing-binary eclipse, so the best explanation is a blended binary, not a planet on the target.

reasons.why: Difference imaging puts the dip ~9.7" from the target at 5.2 sigma, not on the target. This is positive evidence the signal is not on the target star, but on a nearby blended source.
Two stars inside one TESS pixel can produce the 267.3 ppm dip with a <25% eclipse, making a blended EB at 18-21" the plausible cause of the off-target centroid.

Depth changes by ~279% between sectors, with formal non-detections in sectors 53, 59, 79 and very high depths in 73. Alone this can be systematics, but together with no clear on-target centroid it favours a blended source with aperture-dependent contamination rather than a planet with a stable depth.

Secondary at ~38% orbital phase and odd/even differences (2 sectors >3 sigma) plus a V shape (b~0.9639, density penalty 6.195) are not strong for a 1.471 Rearth planet; they align with a diluted EB/bblend, though centroid is the decisive piece.
